title: Jensen Huang’s daughter Madison insulted employees as ‘dead-face’ and ‘goldfish,’ drove top talent away: reports
excerpt: The 35-year-old ex-sommelier and cooking student quickly rose through the ranks at Nvidia after joining in 2020 as an intern.
content_html:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Madison Huang – daughter of disgraced former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang – could be just as demanding as her father, berating longtime employees as “dead-face” or “goldfish” and balking at any criticism, according to a report. 

The 35-year-old ex-sommelier and cooking student quickly rose through the ranks at Nvidia after joining in 2020 as an intern.

Officially a director of marketing, Madison became her father’s de facto chief of staff, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times. 

Madison often yelled in group meetings — both at execs who were more experienced than her and at her own brother, 36-year-old Spencer, a fellow Nvidia employee known for a quiet demeanor, according to people who worked with her.

Nvidia employees estimated that more than a dozen key executives have fled the chipmaker because of Madison, the New York Times reported. 

In a meeting late last year, as Madison was yelling at others on Nvidia’s marketing team, a vice president had a panic attack and had to drop the call, according to two people familiar with the meeting. 

Despite tensions over Madison’s rapid rise at the company, along with her husband Nico Caprez, Jensen Huang and his family were treated like a “royal family” at Nvidia, according to the Wall Street Journal. 

Jensen, 63, could be a similarly harsh boss – but he was also a charismatic leader. He gave afternoon speeches at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus with a glass of wine in hand and would take selfies with new workers wearing his signature black leather jacket, according to the Wall Street Journal. 

So it was a stunning blow to the company when Jensen resigned last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as reports surfaced of at least two more affairs with Nvidia employees. 

Prior to news of his scandalous affairs, Jensen frequently praised his wife and college sweetheart, Lori, for her support – telling employees that he headed home each day at 6:30 p.m. to a dinner made by her, the Journal reported. 

Here’s the latest on the Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy:

  • California AG Rob Bonta serves Nvidia with subpoena in wake of ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s Chinese spy, affairs scandals
  • Trump’s portfolio traded Nvidia five times in September — months before CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal-ridden exit
  • Alarming reason China is desperately seeking US Nvidia chips: ‘Intelligentized warfare’
  • Nvidia exec reportedly berated by Jensen Huang faces scandal as his wife is accused of chip smuggling

Madison told a colleague that her parents were building a compound where the family could all live together, and public records showed an entity linked to Jensen had purchased a $23.6 million home on acreage near Silicon Valley, the report said. 

Though widely admired, Jensen reportedly could be a difficult boss, berating employees in company meetings. Those included CFO Colette Kress – now the interim CEO – whom he reportedly called a “deer in the headlights.”

He often used the term “dead-face” to insult staffers who wore a blank expression on their faces after being lectured in group meetings, and would tell workers point-blank “your question is stupid” or “this idea is stupid,” according to the Journal. 

Like her father, Madison used the term “dead-face” to insult employees, or “goldfish” if they couldn’t remember something, according to employees at the chipmaker. 

“It’s really such a privilege, because it is a family business,” Madison told students at Seoul National University during an appearance earlier this year. “Not just because I get to work with my own family, but because the Nvidia employees, we are like one big family.”

Jensen was aware of his daughter’s behavior, occasionally threatening to sic an angry Madison on other employees – telling them they should be afraid of her, two people familiar with the remarks told the Times. 

Madison and her husband Caprez – a former ski racer whom she met in business school in London – leveraged their close ties to Jensen over more senior employees, according to reports. 

During group meetings, it was clear the couple knew information other people were hearing for the first time, and even senior executives felt they could not disagree with Madison because of her direct line to her dad, according to former senior executives. 

In one instance in February, Madison yelled at other employees – including Jay Puri, a longtime Nvidia staffer set to take Jensen’s place headlining a conference in New Delhi – for being unprepared, according to the Times.

At one point, Puri interrupted and said he could answer Madison’s questions if she stopped yelling at him, the report said. He left his role at Nvidia less than six months later. 

Even in large company meetings, Madison had a reputation for asking uncomfortable questions – prompting several HR complaints about her behavior, though it’s unclear if any action was ever taken, according to the Times. 

Some colleagues defended Madison, saying she could be intense but it was all for the betterment of the company, co-workers told the Journal. Others compared her to a chef or coach with high expectations of their team. 

Madison’s role at the company has raised concerns over potential conflicted loyalties, according to reports – especially amid rumors that Jensen is preparing a comeback campaign. 

His daughter played a central role in hiring a crisis communications firm to focus on her family’s public image in May 2025, arguing the company wasn’t doing enough to protect Jensen’s reputation, according to the New York Times.

Madison, Caprez and Nvidia did not immediately respond to The Post’s requests for comment.
